summary:
No local Ulsan ordinance, directive or enforcement practice concerning trans people appears in the available sources; the national framework of South Korea governs the city directly. South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and no criminal provision is applied against visitors on the basis of gender presentation.

Trans visitors hold a judicially enforced right to public restrooms in Ulsan. On 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the government's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a 3 million won claim, ruling that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed her personal rights. The court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The judgment is final, there is no appeal route remaining, and it binds in Ulsan; the sources record no specific incident in the city.

An earlier judgment points the same way. In 2021 the Daegu District Court's Pohang branch awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom.

Legal gender recognition is available to people in Ulsan without a surgical prerequisite. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that gender change cannot be determined by surgery and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are reference material rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. That ruling governs Ulsan, and the report carries no Ulsan-specific content of its own.
tangentialFactors:
Restroom avoidance is a documented national pattern rather than an isolated grievance. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found that 41% used a restroom belonging to a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink in order to delay the need, and 36% went without using a restroom at all. Visitors should expect the legal right to coexist with habits of avoidance formed under earlier practice.

Hostility at organised public events has been recorded elsewhere in South Korea. In Incheon a Pride event ended in violence when about 1,000 Christian protestors attacked participants, and organisers later filed charges against pastors while accusing police of inaction; at Busan's 2018 Pride, some 2,000 police were deployed to protect 15,000 attendees from violent anti-gay protesters. No comparable event-level violence is documented in the Ulsan sources.

School settings show the same pressure on facilities. Research from the youth LGBTQ+ centre DDing Dong, presented on 20 March 2024, found that trans teenagers avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed, with one 16-year-old trans girl at a boys' school reporting that she holds in and leaves school early. The finding is national and bears on residents rather than short-term visitors.

The military dimension of South Korea's regime does not reach visitors. Transgender people are excluded from military service, and the Military Criminal Act article 92-6, upheld by the Constitutional Court in 2023, criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ulsan seeking a registered-sex change can now petition on the strength of the Yeongdong ruling of 8 May 2024: sex-reassignment surgery is not a precondition, hormonal treatment alone was accepted as the basis for the five applicants, and the judicial guidelines that once demanded surgery are treated as reference rather than binding criteria. The family register entry, once changed, is what the restroom judgment of 22 July 2024 relied on when it protected restroom use aligned with a person's registered sex.

Remedies exist locally. Damages for exclusion from a sex-designated facility have been granted at first instance and confirmed on appeal, and the state itself has been ordered to pay for police advice that told a trans woman to stay out of women's restrooms. The 7 million won award against a beauty academy in 2021 shows that private operators have been liable too.

Healthcare carries an official gap acknowledged within the state. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea identified a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, arguing that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

South Korean national law provides no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no Ulsan ordinance filling that gap is documented. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognised nationally, and same-sex couples cannot adopt jointly.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ulsan-specific court decision, municipal policy, police directive or documented incident involving a trans person appears in the available sources; whether the Ulsan District Court or the city's schools and facilities have handled such matters is unresolved.

The restroom-avoidance percentages come from a 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey with national coverage. A breakdown for Ulsan is not sourced, so the city-level prevalence of avoidance is unknown.

Practical details for visitors and residents in Ulsan are not sourced: the availability of transition-related care in the city, the process and processing time for a local gender-marker change on identity documents, and which public and private facilities in Ulsan have trans-inclusive access policies. Nothing in the inventory confirms or rules these out.

Whether the Yeongdong reasoning of 8 May 2024 has been cited by courts in Ulsan, and whether any appeal or further guideline revision followed it, is unresolved on the present sources.
